Semenov et al. (2026) on dandiset 001515¶

Paper. Semenov I, Silkuniene G, Silkunas M, Pakhomova ON, Bixler JN, Ibey BL, Kochunov P, Pakhomov AG (2026). Sub-microsecond optical measurements of cell membrane charging and lesioning by pulsed electric fields. Bioelectrochemistry 171, 109283. doi:10.1016/j.bioelechem.2026.109283. The claims file (claims/001515/10.1016-j.bioelechem.2026.109283.yaml) was written from the version of record (main text, Methods, Results, Discussion and the figure legends; the paper names no supplement and links no code).

Dandiset. DANDI:001515, version 0.261006.1841, "Plasma Membrane Polarization Dynamics of CHO Cells During 1 us Pulses: Effects of Cell Size and Electric Field Strength". The paper cites no dataset ("Data will be made available on request"). This is the only published version, and the most recent; the draft holds the same files (compared below), so the choice cannot change a result.

What the dandiset holds. 292 NWB files from 37 subjects in four sessions (2023-05-08 to 2023-10-10). Each holds one 70-frame strobe image series of a field of CHO cells loaded with FluoVolt, exposed to single 1-us pulses at one amplitude (20 to 100 V across electrodes 1.00 mm apart), recorded "forward" or "backward", with the anode above or below. The data check below shows that the frames sample the time course of membrane charging and discharging (the frame order runs backward in the "backward" files). This is the time-course protocol the paper attributes to its reference [20] (Semenov et al., Bioelectrochemistry 168 (2025) 109143; Discussion: "similar to what we have reported recently using weaker, non-electroporating PEFs [20]"). None of this paper's experiments is in it: no sets of 40 baseline and 60 pulse images at 900 ns, no field escalation within a cell, no Di-8-ANEPPS, 0.3-us pulses, Gd3+, two-pulse or Fluo-4 recordings. The files do not record the delay of each frame or the field strength in V/cm, and the electrode spacing (1.00 mm) differs from the paper's (1.6 mm).

Claims. 34 claims. One, fig5b-conductivity-calibration, is a computation from the paper's Eq. (2) and uses no recordings; it is tested. The other 33 are blocked, data_missing.

import collections
import time
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from dandi.dandiapi import DandiAPIClient

import strobe

pd.set_option("display.width", 220)
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 40)
pd.set_option("display.max_rows", 400)

started = time.time()
assets = strobe.assets()
with ProcessPoolExecutor(6) as pool:
    meta = pd.DataFrame(list(pool.map(strobe.read_metadata, assets)))
print(f"{len(assets)} NWB files at dandiset {strobe.DANDISET_ID} version {strobe.DANDISET_VERSION}; "
      f"metadata read in {time.time() - started:.0f} s")

ImageSeries description: Optical time-lapse (strobe imaging) recordings of plasma membrane (PM) polarization were performed at 6 Hz (image frames were taken at this rate, but the data represent events occurring at MHz rates). Exposures began 1 µs after the start of recording for single pulse exposures and immediately at the start of the recordings for sine wave exposures. The strobe imaging method utilizes pulsed laser fluorescence microscopy, where a single short-pulse laser flash is delivered at a precise time interval before, during, or after the event (application of an electric pulse (EP)). Cells were pre-loaded with a voltage-sensitive dye (see dye used in session description), which responds to transmembrane potential changes within nanoseconds.

Session description: Subject ID: CHO_20230508_c1. Stimulation was applied with a single 1 µs long rectangular pulse at 40V amplitude . Distance between electrodes 1.00 mm, electrode diameter 0.5 mm. The recording was performed in a forward manner, following the sequence of pulse application to mimic the real-time progression of events. Anode positioned below the cell. CHO polarization were visualized using the voltage-sensitive fluorescent dye FluoVolt and a FITC filter cube. All experiments were performed in standard physiological solution containing (in mM): 140 NaCl, 5.4 KCl, 2 CaCl2, 1.5 MgCl2, 10 D-glucose, and 10 HEPES (pH 7.3, 290-300 mOsm/kg). CHO cells were seeded in culture dishes with 20 mm glass window 1 h before the experiment to maintain spherical shape. More method details in the related manuscript.

Every file holds one image series and nothing else: no stimulus series, no trial or epoch table, no processed data, no per-frame timestamps (only a start time and the stated 6 Hz), and no field strength or laser delay. The species in the archive summary, "Cricetulus griseus - Cricetulus aureus", names two species for one CHO cell line (the files give NCBITaxon_10029, C. griseus), and the subject age "P1D" is given for a cell line.

The texts above confirm the parsed fields: every description names FluoVolt, a single 1-us pulse, one amplitude and electrodes 1.00 mm apart. None of the session descriptions names Di-8-ANEPPS, Gd3+, Fluo-4 or calcium, a second pulse or a train, 0.3-us pulses, 900 ns, 1.6-mm electrodes or a field in V/cm. "Sine" occurs only in the series description, shared by all files, and no file's data or session description holds a sine exposure.

The paper's Methods 2.2 to 2.3 describe electrodes 1.6 mm apart, field strengths in V/cm from Sim4Life modelling, flashes at 900 ns (1-us pulses) or 275 ns (0.3-us pulses), and sets of 100 images (40 without the pulse, then 60 with it), with the amplitude escalated set by set within a cell; two dyes, FluoVolt and Di-8-ANEPPS. The files hold none of that structure: 70 frames per file, one amplitude per subject (20 to 100 V), electrodes 1.00 mm apart, FluoVolt only, and no record of what distinguishes the two files of each subject that share an order and an anode side. One subject (CHO-20230925-c1) has 4 files where the others have 8. The series description mentions "sine wave exposures"; no file describes one.

Next every file's pixels are read once (about 2 minutes): a checksum of every frame, the frame brightness, and a membrane polarization index per frame (the module docstring of strobe.py gives its parameters, standard choices for this check, not the paper's).

started = time.time()
with ProcessPoolExecutor(6) as pool:
    summaries = list(pool.map(strobe.summarize_file, assets))
print(f"pixels of {len(summaries)} files read in {time.time() - started:.0f} s")
px = pd.DataFrame([{k: s[k] for k in ["path", "n_cells", "baseline", "peak", "peak_frame", "first_half",
                                      "last_half", "n_half", "min", "max"]} for s in summaries])
px["frame0_ratio"] = [s["frame_mean"][0] / np.median(s["frame_mean"][1:]) for s in summaries]
d = meta.merge(px, on="path")
print("Pixel values over all files: min", d["min"].min(), "max", d["max"].max(), "(uint16, unit n.a.)")
print("Cells found per file (connected parts of the membrane mask of at least", strobe.MIN_CELL_PX, "px):",
      d.n_cells.describe()[["min", "50%", "max"]].to_dict())

where = collections.defaultdict(list)
for s in summaries:
    for i, h in enumerate(s["frame_md5"]):
        where[h].append((s["path"], i))
shared = [v for v in where.values() if len(v) > 1]
print("\nFrames whose pixel values occur in more than one place:", len(shared), "of", sum(len(v) for v in where.values()))

X = np.array([s["mean_image_small"].ravel() for s in summaries])
X = (X - X.mean(1, keepdims=True)) / X.std(1, keepdims=True)
C = X @ X.T / X.shape[1]
subj = d.subject.to_numpy()
same = subj[:, None] == subj[None, :]
np.fill_diagonal(same, False)
other = subj[:, None] != subj[None, :]
within = np.array([np.median(C[i, same[i]]) for i in range(len(d))])
between = np.array([C[i, other[i]].max() for i in range(len(d))])
print("Correlation of each file's mean image (64 x 64) with the other files of its subject, median:",
      f"median over files {np.median(within):.3f}, lowest {within.min():.3f}")
print("Highest correlation with any file of another subject:", f"median {np.median(between):.3f}, max {between.max():.3f}")
odd = d[within < 0.9]
print("Files whose field of view differs from the rest of their subject:")
print(odd[["path", "session_start", "order", "anode", "peak", "n_cells"]].to_string(index=False))
print("\nPer file: cells found, peak index (%), its frame and the half-peak frames:")
print(d[["path", "volts", "order", "anode", "n_cells", "peak", "peak_frame", "first_half", "last_half"]]
      .round(2).to_string(index=False))

sub-CHO-20231010-c9/sub-CHO-20231010-c9_obj-ej5fzg_image.nwb (100 V, forward, anode above): 138 connected parts of the mask, 7 of at least 300 px (n_cells 7)

Mean image shown from 0 to its 99.5th percentile (988); brighter pixels are drawn at the top of the scale.

The mask is the brightest 10% of the mean image, so it covers whole bright cells, their interiors included, more than their membranes alone. A dim cell (lower left) falls mostly outside it, and two pairs of touching cells (parts 1 and 6 in this file) each form a single part. n_cells therefore counts connected parts of the mask, not cells; each part is split at its centroid into the top and bottom halves the index compares. This matters for no claim: the index is used only to check that the files hold time courses whose sign and size follow the stated anode side and amplitude.

The polarization index rises and falls once in each file, over about 19 frames at half its peak. In "forward" files this happens at frames 16 to 34, and in "backward" files at the same frames counted from the end, so the backward recordings hold the same time course in reverse order, as the session descriptions say. The frames are therefore successive laser delays relative to the pulse (the series description: a flash "at a precise time interval before, during, or after" the pulse), but the files do not record the delays. If the 19 frames of half-peak response span the 1-us pulse, the step is about 50 ns and the 70 frames cover about 3.5 us; this is consistent with the data, not shown by them. Which frame is 900 ns into the pulse, the time point every claim of the paper uses, cannot be read from the files. In most files frame 0 is about 0.6 times as bright as the others (median ratio 0.59).

Next the sign of the index against the anode side the session description gives, and its size against the pulse amplitude.

Sign of the index in files stated 'anode above', per session: {('2023-05-08', 1): 30, ('2023-05-08', -1): 2, ('2023-09-25', 1): 3, ('2023-09-25', -1): 35, ('2023-09-26', 1): 1, ('2023-09-26', -1): 39, ('2023-10-10', 1): 17, ('2023-10-10', -1): 19}

In 35 of 37 subjects the sign of the polarization flips with the stated anode side, as it should; 9 files differ in sign from the majority of the other files of their subject with the same stated anode side (listed above; groups with a tied majority are not counted). Across sessions the stated side does not fix the sign: files with "anode above" are brighter at the top in one session and at the bottom in others, and in the 2023-10-10 session the sign changes between subjects. The image orientation relative to the electrodes is not stated, so the cathode-facing pole of a cell cannot be located from the metadata alone, only from the sign of its response (depolarization brightens FluoVolt, Methods 2.3).

In the 2023-10-10 session, one subject per amplitude, the response grows with the pulse amplitude (Spearman rho 1.0 over nine amplitudes), which is consistent with the stated amplitudes. At the same 40 V it differs between sessions (median 25.9% on 2023-05-08, 11.9% on 2023-09-26, 12.8% on 2023-10-10), so amplitude alone does not set the response across sessions. The amplitudes are in volts across the electrodes; the paper's field strengths in V/cm come from a Sim4Life model of its 1.6-mm electrode geometry, so they cannot be assigned to these files.

fig5b-conductivity-calibration¶

By Eq. (2), the effective membrane conductivity barely affects charging while it stays far below cytosol and medium conductivities; a 10-fold rise reduces IMP by about 2% and a 100-fold rise by 12%.

Criterion: Eq. (2) with the constants of Methods 2.3 (lambda_i 0.4 S/m, lambda_o 1.64 S/m, R 8 um, d 5 nm, intact lambda_m 3e-7 S/m); the reduction relative to IMPC under readings (a) 1 - f/1.5 and (b) 1 - f(lambda_m)/f(3e-7 S/m). Expected 2 +- 0.2% (10-fold) and 12 +- 1.2% (100-fold); reproduced when both are within tolerance under one reading. The computation uses no recordings.

In [10]:
c = strobe.CONSTANTS
lm0 = c["lambda_m_intact"]
expected = {10: (2.0, 0.2), 100: (12.0, 1.2)}
rows = []
for fold in [1, 10, 100, 1000]:
    f = strobe.f_factor(fold * lm0)
    rows.append({"fold": fold, "lambda_m S/m": fold * lm0, "f": f,
                 "reduction_a_%": 100 * (1 - f / 1.5),
                 "reduction_b_%": 100 * (1 - f / strobe.f_factor(lm0))})
calib = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print("Constants (Methods 2.3):", c)
print(calib.to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda x: f"{x:.4g}"))
for fold, (value, tol) in expected.items():
    row = calib[calib.fold == fold].iloc[0]
    for reading in ["a", "b"]:
        got = row[f"reduction_{reading}_%"]
        print(f"{fold}-fold, reading ({reading}): {got:.2f}% against {value} +- {tol}: "
              f"{'within' if abs(got - value) <= tol else 'outside'} tolerance")

Result: partially reproduced. With the paper's constants, Eq. (2) gives a 1.33% (reading a) or 1.20% (reading b) reduction of IMP for a 10-fold rise of membrane conductivity, outside 2 +- 0.2%, and 11.87% or 11.75% for a 100-fold rise, inside 12 +- 1.2%. The qualitative statement, that conductivity far below the cytosol and medium values barely affects charging, holds: a 1000-fold rise is needed to reduce IMP by more than half (57.4%). In the grid of radii and membrane thicknesses printed above, no combination puts both values within tolerance under reading (a), so the ~2% is not explained by the approximate constants alone.

Blocked claims¶

The other 33 claims need recordings that are not in the dandiset (header table). The check above shows what is there instead: FluoVolt time courses at one amplitude per cell. Even for the FluoVolt claims (Fig. 2A, 3 and 4A), the dandiset lacks the escalation sets of 40 baseline and 60 pulse images at 900 ns; and to use its time courses in their place would need the delay of each frame and the field strength in V/cm, neither of which the files record.

Summary¶

Claim Outcome
fig5b-conductivity-calibration partially reproduced (10-fold value 1.33% against ~2%; 100-fold value 11.87% against 12%)
the other 33 claims blocked, data_missing

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. Only a computation from Eq. (2) was run, with the paper's constants; no recording of the paper's experiments is in the dandiset.

What was found about the dataset.

  • It names this paper (IsPublishedIn) but holds a different experiment: FluoVolt time courses of charging and discharging at one pulse amplitude per cell, the protocol the paper attributes to its reference [20]. None of the paper's 40 + 60 image sets at 900 ns, field escalations, Di-8-ANEPPS, 0.3-us, Gd3+, two-pulse or Ca2+ recordings is in it.
  • The laser delay of each frame is not recorded; the data show that the frames are successive delays, reversed in "backward" files.
  • Pulses are given in volts with electrodes 1.00 mm apart, where the paper uses 1.6 mm and modelled field strengths in V/cm.
  • Within a subject, two files share each combination of order and anode side, with nothing to tell them apart. One subject has 4 files.
  • One file of CHO-20230926-c1 shows another field of view and was recorded on 2024-12-16.
  • The stated anode side does not fix the sign of the response across sessions, and a few files differ in sign from the majority of the files of their subject with the same stated anode side.
  • Frame 0 is about 0.6 times as bright as the rest in most files (median ratio 0.59).
  • The archive summary names two species for a CHO cell line, and the subjects (cell fields) have an age of "P1D".
